The Black-winged petrel (Pterodroma nigripennis) is a small, abundant gadfly petrel that breeds across the subtropical Pacific, from Lord Howe Island to the Kermadec archipelago. Field studies on Muttonbird Island indicate that eggs are incubated at a mean temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], producing a hatchling that emerges after approximately 45.3 days [ab = approximately 45.3 days]. This incubation period is relatively extended compared to other Procellariiformes of similar egg size, a pattern often attributed to the burrow-nesting habit and the buffering capacity of the subterranean thermal environment. Upon hatching, the altricial neonate is covered in fine down and weighs just 33 grams [Wwb = 33 grams], a modest initial mass that reflects the limited yolk reserves typical of petrels. This low neonatal body mass imposes a heavy demand on biparental provisioning throughout the subsequent nestling phase, as the chick must accumulate substantial tissue reserves to meet the energetic requirements of fledging and post-fledging survival.

During the nestling period, which spans several months, the chick undergoes a dramatic transformation in body composition and size. Under the thermal regime typical of active metabolic periods for this species, approximately 39.4 °C [T = approximately 39.4 °C], the developing nestling attains an asymptotic body mass of 350 grams [Wwi = 350 grams] shortly before fledging. This ultimate wet weight, representing more than a tenfold increase from the hatching mass, is achieved through the regular delivery of high-lipid stomach oil by both parents. The fledging event itself, marking the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the burrow, occurs at 85 days after hatching [tx = 85 days after hatching] when maintained at 39.4 °C at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].

Following fledging, juveniles enter a prolonged period of oceanic dispersal and somatic growth before reaching reproductive competence. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal maturation, is attained at 255 days after hatching [tp = 255 days after hatching] under the thermal conditions of 39.4 °C typical of active thermoregulation in adults at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This relatively rapid sexual maturation, within the first year of life, is unusual among the Procellariidae, where many species delay reproduction for several years. However, despite reaching physiological maturity at this early age, first breeding is typically deferred considerably, with individuals not initiating reproduction until approximately 2 to 3 years after hatching. This gap between the attainment of puberty and the onset of reproductive activity is thought to reflect the time required for young birds to acquire the foraging skills, body condition, and social standing necessary to successfully compete for burrow sites and mates.

The onset of first reproduction in Black-winged petrel is a critical demographic milestone that shapes population dynamics. The time since birth at first brood has been recorded at 730 days [tR = 730 days] at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], a value that corresponds to the lower end of the 2 to 3 year range reported across the species' range. Reproductive output is modest: females typically produce a single egg per breeding attempt [N_R_i = single egg per breeding attempt], and given the constraints of the long incubation and chick-rearing period, they achieve a maximum of only one successful clutch per year [F_R_i = one successful clutch per year], resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of one egg per year [Ri = one egg per year]. This combination of low fecundity per event and infrequent annual breeding is typical of the slow life-history pace that characterizes most oceanic seabirds. The annual reproductive effort is thus heavily concentrated into a single, high-investment offspring, reflecting the trade-off between current reproduction and adult survival in a resource-poor pelagic environment.

Longevity data for the Black-winged petrel indicate a remarkably extended lifespan for a bird of its body size. Field records from long-term banding studies on the Kermadec Islands show that the maximum lifespan in the wild reaches approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years], with individuals documented to live over two decades under favorable conditions at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. When expressed in terms of total lifetime reproductive output at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], this extreme longevity partially compensates for the species' low annual fecundity, as a single long-lived adult can produce numerous offspring over its breeding lifespan. Comparative analysis with other Pterodroma species suggests that this extended lifespan is an adaptive response to the high environmental stochasticity and unpredictable food availability characteristic of the subtropical ocean gyres. Such a life-history strategy, combining late maturation, low fecundity, and high adult survival, aligns with the broader syndrome observed across the Procellariiformes.
